lede: Put a list in order and the median cuts it in half. Cut each half in half again and you have the quartiles: three marks that split the data into four equal groups. The gap between the outer two is the interquartile range, the width of the middle half.
can: Order a list and work the three quartile positions out from $n$.
Read a quartile whose position falls halfway between two values.
Use the interquartile range to say which set is more consistent.

text: Quartiles: three cuts, four equal groups

md: The median splits ordered data in half. Two more cuts, one halfway down each half, split it into four groups of equal size. Those two extra cuts are the **lower quartile** and the **upper quartile**, and the distance between them is the **interquartile range**, the width of the middle half. That width is the point of the idea, because the range is decided by the two most unusual values in the set.

prompt: How many values lie between the lower quartile and the upper quartile?
explain: The quartiles are the first and third cuts, so the middle two groups, half of the data, sit between them.

md:
A quartile is a **position** in the ordered data, so the order comes first and the counting second.

1. Write the values out again from smallest to largest.
2. Count them: that is $n$.
3. Lower quartile at position $\tfrac{1}{4}(n+1)$, median at $\tfrac{1}{2}(n+1)$, upper quartile at $\tfrac{3}{4}(n+1)$.
4. Read the value at each position.
5. Interquartile range $=$ upper quartile $-$ lower quartile.

With $n = 11$ the positions are $3$, $6$ and $9$: three whole numbers, because $n+1$ divides by four.

prompt: A list has 15 values in order. At which position is the upper quartile?
explain: $\tfrac{3}{4}(15 + 1) = 12$, so the upper quartile is the 12th value.

title: Not on the formula sheet
md:
$\text{LQ at } \tfrac{1}{4}(n+1), \quad \text{median at } \tfrac{1}{2}(n+1), \quad \text{UQ at } \tfrac{3}{4}(n+1)$

$\text{IQR} = \text{UQ} - \text{LQ}$

The page-2 Higher formula sheet carries no statistics formulae at all, so all four of these are recall.

prompt: Using the picture above, what is the interquartile range of the waiting times, in minutes?

text: When the position is not a whole number

md:
With $n = 9$ the lower quartile position is $\tfrac{1}{4}(9+1) = 2.5$. There is no 2.5th value, so read it the way you read a point between two marks on a ruler: go halfway from the 2nd value to the 3rd, which is their mean.

For the seed potatoes $12, 14, 15, 18, 20, 23, 25, 28, 34$: the 2nd and 3rd masses are $14$ and $15$, so LQ $= 14.5$ kg. Rounding the position to 2 or to 3 is the common slip, and it moves the answer.

prompt: For the same nine masses ($12, 14, 15, 18, 20, 23, 25, 28, 34$) the upper quartile is at position 7.5. What is the upper quartile, in kg?
explain: Halfway between the 7th and 8th masses: $\dfrac{25 + 28}{2} = 26.5$ kg.

title: Quartiles from a List
why: Five minutes of worked lists at different sizes of n. Watch how the positions are written down before any value is read; that line is what earns the first mark.

prompt: In the video, what is written down before any quartile value is read off?
explain: Yes. The positions come from n, and the values are only read once the positions are settled.

text: What the interquartile range is for

md:
Two data sets can share a median and still be nothing alike. A **smaller** interquartile range means the middle half of the values sit closer together, so the data is more **consistent**.

It also survives an extreme value. Eleven trains leave late by $3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8$ and $58$ minutes. The range is $55$ minutes, which describes no ordinary morning. The quartiles are the 3rd and 9th values, $4$ and $7$, so the interquartile range is $3$ minutes: the honest picture of a typical delay.

prompt: Eleven trains are late by $3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8$ and $58$ minutes. What is the range, in minutes?
explain: $58 - 3 = 55$, which describes no ordinary morning. The interquartile range of 3 minutes is the honest picture of a typical delay.

title: Why the extreme value cannot reach the quartiles
md: The range is built from positions $1$ and $n$, the two ends. The quartiles sit a quarter and three quarters of the way in, so changing the largest value to $58$, or to $580$, moves it further out but never changes which value sits at position 9.

prompt: Two bakeries have the same median loaf mass. Bakery A has an interquartile range of 6 g and bakery B one of 21 g. Which statement earns the mark?
options: Bakery A is more consistent, because the middle half of its loaves vary by only 6 g
Bakery A has heavier loaves on average
answer: Bakery A is more consistent, because the middle half of its loaves vary by only 6 g
explain: The medians are equal, so neither is heavier on average. The interquartile range is a measure of spread, and the smaller one means less variation.

title: A reason has to point at this data
md: November 2025 M3 Q26(b) asked why the interquartile range represented a data set better than the range, and it was the poorest-answered item on the paper. General contrasts of range and interquartile range scored nothing. The mark needed the observation that one very high value, 98%, had inflated the range. Name the value in front of you.

prompt: Fill the gap: interquartile range = upper quartile − ______ quartile.
explain: Upper quartile minus lower quartile. Subtracting the median instead measures only half the middle.

Order the list, then work the three positions out from $n$.
Read a quartile whose position falls between two values.
Subtract for the interquartile range, and say what it shows.

The wording is short: Calculate, the statistic named in full, then a bare list and a two-mark answer line. The first mark is the two quartiles, the second the subtraction. Write three lines every time — the ordered list, the two quartiles, then the subtraction with its unit. Stuck: order the list and write the positions; a correct position line with one quartile beats a blank.
